title: The Chameleon Effect
text:
In 1999 Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh of New York University published a set of experiments on how people unconsciously copy each other. In the first, students worked on a task of describing photographs with a partner who was actually a member of the research team. Some partners kept rubbing their faces; others kept shaking a foot. Hidden cameras recorded the participants, who began to rub their own faces or shake their own feet more, depending on which partner they were with. Almost none noticed doing it.

In the second experiment the roles were reversed. This time the research assistant quietly mirrored the participant's posture, gestures and mannerisms during the conversation, or simply behaved neutrally. Participants who had been mirrored liked the assistant more and said the interaction had gone more smoothly, without realizing they had been imitated.

A third study found that people who scored higher on a measure of perspective taking, the habit of trying to see things from others' viewpoints, mimicked others more. Chartrand and Bargh named the pattern the chameleon effect and suggested that this automatic mimicry acts as a kind of social glue, building rapport between people who interact.
lesson: People bond partly through small, unconscious echoes of each other's behavior. Paying real attention to someone tends to bring you into step with them naturally.
location: New York University, New York, USA
source: Chartrand, T. L., and Bargh, J. A. (1999). The chameleon effect: The perception-behavior link and social interaction. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 76(6), 893-910.
